1338.title: Why Kunti walked away
1338.hook: her sons finally rule, and Kunti walks into the forest: the Hindu stage of life for letting go
1338.carry: vanaprastha: a season for letting go
1338.tomorrow: The blessing that names no side
1338.howItsDone: The four stages of life, the ashramas, are set out in Hindu law books such as the Laws of Manu; few people now leave for a real forest, but many Hindu grandparents step back from running the household and give their days to prayer, temple and pilgrimage, which many teachers describe as vanaprastha today.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-EIGHT.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, your own dharma is faced, not avoided: Kunti sent her sons the story of Vidula, better to blaze for a moment than to smolder for a long time.
screen: `YOUR OWN DHARMA IS FACED, NOT AVOIDED.`

segments.voice: A small procession leaves Hastinapura through the gate. In it walks an old blind king, Dhritarashtra, whose sons died in the war. His hand rests on the shoulder of his wife, Gandhari, her eyes bound with cloth. And Gandhari's hand rests on the shoulder of the woman leading them both: Kunti. The Pandavas are on the throne at last. Their mother has everything the war was fought for, and she is walking away from it, into the forest, guiding the parents of the men her sons killed. Her sons run after her. Today: Kunti's last word to them.
screen: `A PROCESSION LEAVES THE CITY.` → `A HAND ON EACH SHOULDER.` → `KUNTI LEADS THEM OUT.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Mahabharata's Book of the Hermitage. Dhritarashtra has decided to end his days in the forest, and Gandhari goes with him. Kunti's sons assume their mother will stay. She doesn't. Bhima puts the hard question into words, in paraphrase: you roused us to fight, and now that the kingdom is ours, you leave it? Kunti's answer is the center of the scene. I urged you on so that you wouldn't live in humiliation, so that Draupadi would not be wronged again. Not so that I could enjoy a kingdom. I had my time as a queen, with your father. Now I will serve my elders in the forest. Go back. Here's the teaching. Hindu law books describe life in four stages, the ashramas: student, householder, then vanaprastha, the forest-dweller, and last the renouncer. The Laws of Manu put it simply: when a householder sees wrinkles, gray hair and his children's children, it is time for the forest. Vanaprastha means stepping back from running the house and the money and the fights, and turning the rest of life toward God. Kunti fought hard in her householder's season, for duty, not the prize, so when the season turns, there's nothing she needs to hold. Few Hindus walk into a real forest now. But you'll see the stage in plenty of families: a grandparent who hands over the kitchen and the keys and spends the mornings at the temple or on pilgrimage. Many teachers read that as vanaprastha, kept the modern way.
screen: `SHE LEAVES THE KINGDOM BEHIND` · `NOT FOR MY OWN ENJOYMENT` · `FOUR STAGES OF LIFE` · `VANAPRASTHA: A TIME TO LET GO`

segments.voice: Rest one hand lightly on your own shoulder, the way Gandhari's rested on Kunti's, and bring to mind one thing you're holding tightly in this season of your life: a role, a say in things, a plan. Ask gently whether it's yours to keep, or one day yours to hand on. Stay with that for a few breaths without deciding anything. If you pray, you can offer it to God; if you don't, just loosen your grip on it for a moment.
Kunti. With the kingdom won, she walked into the forest, guiding Gandhari, and told her sons she had urged them on for their honor, not her own enjoyment. Today's word.

1339.title: The blessing that names no side
1339.hook: her son asks for a blessing to win, and Gandhari blesses dharma instead
1339.carry: where dharma is, there is victory
1339.howItsDone: Hindus hear Gandhari's words in retellings of the Mahabharata; the phrase yato dharmas tato jayah is the motto of the Supreme Court of India.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-THIRTY-NINE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, vanaprastha, a season for letting go: Kunti walked out of the city with the kingdom won, guiding Gandhari, whose hand rested on her shoulder.
screen: `VANAPRASTHA: A SEASON FOR LETTING GO.`

segments.voice: A mother's blessing, before a fight, is supposed to be easy. Go well. Come home. Win. During the war, the Mahabharata says, Duryodhana came to his mother Gandhari and asked for her blessing for victory. He was her son. He was fighting for his life and his crown. All she had to say was, may you win. She never said it. Today Gandhari gets her own days, starting with the words she gave him instead.
screen: `A SON ASKS FOR A BLESSING.` → `MAY YOU WIN.` → `SHE NEVER SAID IT.`

segments.voice: Her answer is a short line in Sanskrit: yato dharmas tato jayah. Where dharma is, there is victory. It's a blessing that refuses to take sides by name. If Duryodhana is in the right, it's a blessing. If he isn't, it's a warning. And it wasn't the first time she said hard things to him. Before the war, in the Book of Effort, she is called into the royal court while Krishna's peace mission is failing. She speaks to her son in front of everyone, in paraphrase: a person who can't rule his own senses can't rule a kingdom for long. Make peace with your cousins. Duryodhana walks out of the hall. Here's the teaching under both scenes. Dharma, the right order of things, stands above my side and your side, even above a mother's love for her son. Gandhari doesn't stop being his mother; she just won't pray for anything but what's right. And the line outlives her. After the war, when grief makes her want to curse the victors, the epic reminds her of her own words. Today, yato dharmas tato jayah is the motto of the Supreme Court of India, written on its emblem: a mother's answer before a battle, now over the country's highest court. And it's how many Hindu families pray before an exam, a match, a court date: not just let me win, but let what's right win, and let me be on that side.
screen: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY` · `SHE WARNS HIM IN OPEN COURT` · `DHARMA ABOVE ANY SIDE` · `THE MOTTO OF INDIA'S SUPREME COURT`

1340.title: Why Gandhari tied the cloth
1340.hook: a bride binds her eyes for her blind husband, and Hindus have argued about the pativrata ever since
1340.carry: the devoted wife: honored, and questioned
1340.tomorrow: The night the river gave back the dead
1340.howItsDone: Hindus meet Gandhari's blindfold in retellings of the Mahabharata on stage and screen, where it is held up as the devotion of a pativrata, a devoted wife; the same ideal stands behind fasts some wives keep for their husbands, and many Hindus today also question it.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, where dharma is, there is victory: Gandhari's answer to her son before battle.
screen: `WHERE DHARMA IS, THERE IS VICTORY.`

segments.voice: Paintings show it. So do films and television. A strip of cloth, tied over Gandhari's eyes. A princess of Gandhara learns that the prince she will marry, Dhritarashtra, is blind, and she binds her own eyes. The Mahabharata tells it in a few lines and moves on. Hindus haven't moved on. Today: the cloth, the old ideal it stands for, and the honest argument about it.
screen: `A STRIP OF CLOTH.` → `A FEW LINES IN THE EPIC.` → `HINDUS HAVEN'T MOVED ON.`

segments.voice: Here's what the first book of the Mahabharata gives, in paraphrase. Gandhari hears that her husband-to-be is blind. She takes a cloth, folds it over, and binds her eyes, resolving not to go beyond her husband. No speech. Now the teaching. The cloth is the most famous picture of an old Hindu ideal: the pativrata, the wife wholly devoted to her husband. The epic takes that ideal seriously. Its forest book has a whole section named for the greatness of the devoted wife, and Savitri's story, later this week, sits inside it. And the tradition believed such devotion, kept like a vow, built real power, the same heat of self-discipline, tapas, that sages win in the forest. The epic shows it. After the war, when Yudhishthira bows before her, grieving and angry, Gandhari's eyes fall through a gap in the cloth onto his toes, and his nails turn dark. Later retellings add that one look from her could have made Duryodhana's body hard as diamond. That's the ideal honored. Now the question, and it's an old one too: a woman of clear sight chose not to look, at a court that badly needed someone to look, while her sons went wrong. Many modern Hindus, and many devout ones, hold both: the devotion was real and powerful, and seeing clearly is part of dharma too. That's why the ideal is still argued over in Hindu homes, around fasts wives keep for husbands, and why plenty of families now read devotion as something both partners owe.
screen: `SHE BINDS HER OWN EYES` · `THE PATIVRATA: THE DEVOTED WIFE` · `DEVOTION AS TAPAS, AS POWER` · `BUT DHARMA ALSO NEEDS EYES OPEN`

segments.voice: If you're somewhere safe, close your eyes or rest a hand gently over them, and notice how the room changes: the sounds come closer, the body gets louder. After a few breaths, bring to mind someone you're devoted to, and ask one quiet question: is there something about them, or about us, I've chosen not to see? Don't solve it now; just let your eyes open slowly. If you pray, you can ask for devotion that sees clearly.
Gandhari. Hearing her husband was blind, she bound her own eyes, and became the epic's most famous picture of the devoted wife, honored and questioned. Today's word.

1341.title: The night the river gave back the dead
1341.hook: Gandhari asks to see her sons once more, and for one night the river where Hindus offer water to the dead gives them back
1341.carry: tarpan: water offered to the ones we lost
1341.howItsDone: Hindu families offer water to the dead, tarpan, often with sesame seeds, at a river such as the Ganga or at home, as part of shraddha rites on death anniversaries and during Pitru Paksha, the fortnight for the ancestors.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the devoted wife, honored and questioned: Gandhari's blindfold, one folded cloth, read as devotion, solidarity and a refusal to look.
screen: `THE DEVOTED WIFE: HONORED, AND QUESTIONED.`

segments.voice: Night on the bank of the Ganga. An old blind king, his wife with her eyes bound, and Kunti beside them sit in the dark with the Pandavas and the widows of the war, waiting. The sage Vyasa has told them to bathe and wait. They are waiting for the dead. It began with Gandhari. In the forest, the Mahabharata says, when Vyasa came to visit, she spoke to him of her grief, and asked whether her sons, and the sons of all those mothers, could be seen once more. Today, the last of Gandhari's days: the night the river gave them back.
screen: `NIGHT ON THE GANGA'S BANK.` → `WAITING FOR THE DEAD.` → `IT BEGAN WITH GANDHARI'S REQUEST.`

segments.voice: The scene is in the Book of the Hermitage, here in paraphrase. When night comes, Vyasa goes into the river and calls the fallen warriors by name. They rise out of the water, warriors of both sides, as they looked in life, and the text is careful about one thing: they come without anger. Fathers meet sons, wives meet husbands. Kunti sees Karna. And Gandhari, for this one night, sees her sons. At dawn the warriors go back into the river, each to the world his deeds have earned. Why the river? Because it's where the living had already met the dead. Right after the war, the epic says, the families went down to the Ganga and poured out water for the fallen, and Kunti asked them to pour it for Karna too. That's one of the oldest Hindu rites, still kept: tarpan, offering water, often with sesame, to those who have died, part of the memorial rites called shraddha. Families do it at a river or at home, on a death anniversary and in the fortnight for the ancestors, Pitru Paksha. The teaching inside it: the dead go on, each by their karma, and the bond with them isn't cut. We keep it with water and with their names. The epic doesn't pretend grief can be undone, only that it can be met, in peace. Later, a forest fire comes, and the old king, Gandhari and Kunti meet it sitting still, and are gone together.
screen: `VYASA CALLS THE WARRIORS BY NAME` · `THEY RISE WITHOUT ANGER` · `WATER FOR THE DEAD: TARPAN` · `THE BOND ISN'T CUT`

segments.voice: If there's someone you've lost, let them come to mind gently, as they looked when they were well, and say their name once, quietly. If there's a glass of water nearby, hold it a moment in their honor, the way families pour water at the river. When you're ready, let them go back, the way the warriors returned at dawn, and if you pray, you can commend them to God's keeping. If grief ever feels like more than you can carry, please reach out: in the US, call or text 988, or your local emergency number.
Gandhari. In the forest she asked only to see her sons again, and for one night by the Ganga the dead rose without anger. Today's word.

segments.voice: A verse with a second name. Earlier this year, the verse to the sun that people call the Gayatri turned up in the older law books as the Savitri, the verse to the god Savitr. Keep that name in your pocket. In the Mahabharata, a sage sitting with the exiled Pandavas in the forest tells of a king with no child, and the verse he keeps offering with is that one. Last year we heard Savitri's whole story. This time we stay with the woman herself, starting where she starts: with her name.
screen: `THE GAYATRI HAS A SECOND NAME.` → `A KING WITH NO CHILD.` → `WHERE HER NAME CAME FROM.`

segments.voice: The king is Ashvapati, ruler of the Madras. The epic calls him good, truthful and generous, and grieved by one thing: there is no child in his house. So he takes up a discipline. He eats sparingly and keeps his senses in check. Again and again, into the sacred fire, he makes offerings with the Savitri verse, and he keeps it up a long time. Then one day the fire answers. The goddess Savitri herself rises out of it, pleased with him, and offers him a gift. He asks for children. She tells him a daughter will be born to him, full of radiance. When the girl comes, the king names her after the goddess who gave her: Savitri. Now the teaching, because this verse is the most famous prayer in Hinduism. It's the Gayatri mantra, from the Rig Veda, and what it asks for, in paraphrase, is: may the light of the sun god stir our thoughts. Not wealth, not victory. A mind woken up. That's why it's the verse a teacher whispers to a child at the sacred thread ceremony, and why the daily twilight rite, sandhya, says it at dawn and dusk, while the light is changing. And the girl named for it grows into a woman who keeps her thinking clear under pressure: she chooses her husband, hears a terrible warning without flinching, and stands in front of Death and keeps talking. The epic doesn't spell out the link; many readers hear it anyway. A prayer for a lit mind, made into a woman who keeps her head.
screen: `ASHVAPATI OFFERS WITH THE VERSE` · `THE GODDESS RISES FROM THE FIRE` · `THE GAYATRI: MAY THE LIGHT STIR OUR THOUGHTS` · `SAID AT DAWN AND DUSK`

segments.voice: Sit facing the light, a window or a lamp, and let it fall on your face for a few breaths. If you know the Gayatri and you pray, say it once, silently, the way it's said at dawn and dusk. If you don't, ask in your own words for one clear thought today, and let the breath settle.

1343.title: Savitri's three-night vow
1343.hook: Savitri knows her husband's death day, tells no one, and keeps a vow of fasting for three nights
1343.carry: a vrata: a fast held as prayer for someone
1343.howItsDone: Hindus keep vratas, vows begun with a stated resolve and kept with fasting or restraint, for themselves and often for others: some married women keep a fast in Savitri's name, and parents and grandparents keep weekday or festival fasts for a family member's health or success.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Gayatri asks the light to wake our minds, and Savitri got her name from it: a verse to the sun, a goddess who rose from her father's fire, and a baby named for both.
screen: `THE GAYATRI ASKS THE LIGHT TO WAKE OUR MINDS.`

segments.voice: The warning was spoken once, in a palace. When the sage Narada said that Satyavan would die within the year, he said it at a royal court, to Savitri and her father. Then the wedding happened in a forest hermitage, far from that court. Satyavan didn't hear the warning. His parents didn't. The hermits didn't. So Savitri moves into her new home carrying a sentence about her husband that nobody around her has heard. Today: what she does with it, and what she doesn't say.
screen: `A WARNING, SPOKEN ONCE.` → `NO ONE IN THE HERMITAGE HEARD.` → `SHE CARRIES IT ALONE.`

segments.voice: First, what she does. She takes off her jewels and wears the rough cloth of the forest. She looks after her husband's parents, an old king who has lost his sight and his kingdom, and his wife. And through all of it, the epic says, Narada's words stay in her mind, day and night. She is counting. She doesn't tell Satyavan or his parents. The epic never says why; some readers hear mercy, sparing them a year of dread, some hear resolve. When the day draws near, she does the one thing she can: she takes a vow, a vrata, fasting and standing through three nights. Her father-in-law worries it's too hard. She tells him gently that she will finish it, because it was undertaken with resolve. Here's the teaching. A vrata is one of the most common Hindu practices there is: a vow, begun with a stated resolve, a sankalpa, kept with fasting or restraint, and finished, offered for something you care about. Often for someone else. Savitri's is the most famous; many married women still keep a fast in her name. Mothers and grandmothers fast for a child's health or a grandchild's exam. It isn't a bargain with God, many teachers say; it's prayer you hold in your body, so the person you're praying for is with you all day. And look at Savitri's silence again. She isn't hiding from the truth. She's turning her fear into a vow, eyes open, counting toward the day, getting ready with her own body.
screen: `SHE SERVES AND SHE COUNTS` · `SHE TELLS NO ONE` · `A VRATA: A VOW, A FAST, A RESOLVE` · `PRAYER HELD IN THE BODY`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person you're worried for right now. Make a small resolve for them, a sankalpa, something you can keep today: skip one treat, keep one hour quiet, say one prayer at a set time. Say it inwardly, plainly: today, for them, I'll do this. If you pray, offer it to God; if you don't, let it simply be a way of keeping them with you all day.

1344.title: What Savitri told Death
1344.hook: Savitri has no weapon on the road behind Death, only words about the company of the good
1344.carry: satsang: time near the good is never wasted
1344.howItsDone: Hindus gather for satsang, the company of the good, at temples and in homes, for bhajans, readings and talks; Savitri's words to Yama are heard when her story is retold, and on the day of the vow some married women keep in her name.

screen: `DAY ONE-THOUSAND-THREE-HUNDRED-FORTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday, a vrata, a fast held as prayer for someone: in the hermitage, Savitri carried Narada's warning alone, counted the days, and fasted three nights.
screen: `A VRATA: A FAST HELD AS PRAYER FOR SOMEONE.`

segments.voice: No sword. No army. No spell. When Yama, the lord of death, draws Satyavan's life out of his body and turns south, Savitri has nothing to fight with. What she has is a voice. She walks behind Death and talks, and again and again, Death stops to listen. Last year we followed the boons one by one. Today we listen to what she actually says, because that's what moves him.
screen: `NO SWORD, NO ARMY.` → `SHE WALKS AND TALKS.` → `DEATH STOPS TO LISTEN.`

segments.voice: Yama tells her to turn back. Her first answer is about where she belongs: where her husband is taken, she goes. Then she speaks of friendship. The wise say, she tells him, that walking seven steps together makes people friends, and she has walked more than that beside him. She doesn't plead with Death as an enemy. She claims him as a companion on the road. Then she speaks of dharma, and of the good, the people who keep to it. Yama is pleased and offers a gift, anything but Satyavan's life. She asks for her father-in-law's sight. She keeps talking: being near the good, even for a moment, is never wasted. Another gift: her father-in-law's kingdom. The good are kind even to those who wrong them, she says. Another gift: sons for her own father. And the good, she says, hold the world up by their truth. Each time, what pleases Yama is not grief and not cleverness. It's what she says about goodness. Here's the teaching she's pointing at, one Hindus prize: satsang, the company of the good. Being near holy and good people is held to change you, slowly, the way sitting near a fire warms you. It's why Hindus gather at the temple for bhajans and talks, why families sit together for a reading, why a visit to a holy person is called a blessing. This is a week's end, so look back. Kunti walked into vanaprastha. Gandhari blessed dharma over her own side, bound her eyes, and poured water for her sons. Savitri, named for the Gayatri, kept a vow, and now speaks of the good to Death himself.
screen: `SEVEN STEPS MAKE A FRIEND` · `NEAR THE GOOD IS NEVER WASTED` · `SATSANG: THE COMPANY OF THE GOOD` · `A CONVERSATION DEATH ENJOYS`

segments.voice: Call to mind someone whose goodness you've seen up close, not famous, just good, and one small kind thing they did that nobody else noticed. Sit near them in your mind for a few breaths, the way Savitri says the good are worth being near, and let a little of it rub off. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; this week, you might find a way to spend real time near them.
